description: What is over THERE: given a position and the direction the user is facing, the places inside that cone, and whether the ground and the buildings in between let them actually be seen. Use this for "what is that over there", "is there a pub in that direction", "what am I looking at". Use `nearby_places` instead when the question is about what is NEAR a point rather than what is in a direction. Provide `lat`, `lon`, `bearing_deg` (degrees CLOCKWISE FROM TRUE NORTH: 0 north, 90 east, 180 south, 270 west) and at least one of `category` or `name`; `category=building` reaches named buildings. Optional `fov_deg` is the FULL width of the cone (default 60, so 30 degrees either side), `radius_m` the range (default 1000, max 5000), `eye_height_m` the observer's eye height (default 1.6). Each result carries `distance_m`, `bearing_deg`, a signed `angular_offset_deg` (negative left, positive right), a spoken `direction`, and a `visibility` block. READ THE VISIBILITY BLOCK BEFORE SAYING ANYTHING: `clear` means nothing in the data stands in the way, `occluded` names what does (a hill, or a building with its height), and `unknown` means NO check could run: with `unknown` say you cannot tell, never that it is visible. Read `basis` too: `terrain-only` in a town means hills were checked and buildings were not, which is weak. A non-zero `out_of_sector` means there ARE matching places nearby, just not in that direction, so say that rather than "nothing nearby". `coverage` names the datasets that answered and `caveat` is the standing limit: visibility is modelled from maps, not observed, and trees, walls, scaffolding and weather are not in it. Requires the MapMap gateway (GATEWAY_URL + GATEWAY_API_KEY).

bearing_deg.description:
Which way the observer is facing, in degrees **clockwise from true
north** (0 = north, 90 = east, 180 = south, 270 = west). Required:
this tool answers "what is over there", and "there" has to point
somewhere.

category.description:
The kind of place to look for, from the same vocabulary
`nearby_places` uses ("cafe", "pub", "fuel", "charging_station" …).
Use "building" to ask what a named building over there is. At
least one of `category` and `name` is required.

eye_height_m.description:
Height of the observer's eye above the ground in metres (0–500,
default 1.6, a standing adult). A driver's eye is nearer 1.2 m.

fov_deg.description:
Full width in degrees of the cone centred on `bearing_deg` (1–360,
default 60, so 30 degrees either side). The FULL width, not the
half angle.

lat.description: Latitude of the observer in decimal degrees (−90 to 90).

lon.description: Longitude of the observer in decimal degrees (−180 to 180).

name.description:
A place name or brand to look for. At least one of `category` and
`name` is required.

radius_m.description: Maximum straight-line range in metres (1–5000, default 1000).

visible_only.description:
When true, return only places whose visibility verdict is `clear`.
Default false, which returns everything in the cone WITH its
verdict, usually the better answer, because "it is there but you
cannot see it from here" is worth saying.

name: places_in_view

PlaceInView.description: One place in the observer's field of view.

angular_offset_deg.description:
Signed angle from the observer's bearing to the place: negative to
the left, positive to the right.

bearing_deg.description:
The place's own bearing from the observer, degrees clockwise from
true north.

categories.description: The place's categories as the map tags them.

direction.description:
The direction phrased for speech, from where the observer stands
("ahead and slightly to your right, about 80 metres"). Prefer
reading this aloud over coordinates.

distance_m.description: Straight-line distance from the observer, in metres.

label.description: One-line label: name, street, postcode, town, country.

visibility.description: Whether it can be seen, and what that rests on.

ViewObstruction.description: What stands in the way of seeing a place.

building_height_basis.description:
`tagged` when somebody mapped the building's height, or
`schema-default` when nobody did and the map's flat 5 m fallback
was used. A `schema-default` obstruction is a weaker finding and
should be described as one.

building_height_m.description:
Height of the blocking building above its own ground, in metres.
Absent for terrain.

building_name.description: The blocking building's name, when the map carries one.

distance_m.description: How far along the sight line it stands, in metres.

height_above_sightline_m.description: How far its top rises above the sight line, in metres.

ViewVisibility.description: Whether a place can be seen from the observer, and what that rests on.

basis.description:
What the verdict rests on: `terrain-and-buildings`,
`terrain-only`, `buildings-only` or `nothing`. `terrain-only` in a
town is weak: it means hills were checked and buildings were not.

buildings.description:
What the building check concluded: `clear`, `occluded`,
`no-building-data` or `beyond-building-range`.

obstruction.description: The obstruction, present exactly when the verdict is `occluded`.

terrain.description:
What the terrain check concluded: `clear`, `occluded` or
`no-elevation-data`.

verdict.description:
`clear` (nothing in the data stands in the way), `occluded`
(something does, and it is named), or `unknown` (no check could
run, so this result carries NO visibility claim: say so rather
than implying either).

caveat.description: The standing caveat: visibility here is modelled, not observed.

coverage.description:
One sentence naming which datasets the visibility verdicts were
actually checked against. Worth repeating when a verdict is being
relied on.

out_of_sector.description:
How many otherwise-matching places were dropped for lying outside
the cone. Non-zero means there ARE matching places near the
observer, just not in the direction they are facing, so say that
rather than "nothing nearby".

results.description:
Places inside the cone, best first: everything visible before
everything unchecked before everything occluded, and within each
of those, nearest and most nearly dead-ahead first.
